planting.note: Set out rooted suckers or container-grown plants in spring once soil is workable, in poor, sandy, or saline soil in full sun; American silverberry needs no fertility amendment and spreads by root suckers, so site it where its colonizing habit can be contained away from cultivated beds.

directions: Set out rooted suckers or container plants in spring on poor, sandy, or saline ground where its vigorous, nitrogen-fixing roots and suckering habit can be left to spread without crowding cultivated beds. This silvery-leaved North American native tolerates conditions few other fruiting shrubs can, needing no supplemental fertility once established. Small, fragrant yellow flowers in early summer give way to silvery, mealy berries that ripen in fall and are used for jam, drying, and winter forage for birds. Unlike the related autumn olive and Russian olive, American silverberry is a true native across most of its range and behaves far less aggressively, making it a sound choice for windbreaks, erosion control, and reclamation plantings.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Elaeagnus commutata
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Set out rooted semi-hardwood cuttings or nursery liners in spring after frost danger passes, in sandy, humus-rich, well-drained soil with light afternoon shade in hot climates; midyim tolerates only light, brief frost, so grow it in a movable container at the cold edge of its range.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery liners in spring in sandy, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving light afternoon shade where summers run hot. This low, spreading Australian bush-food shrub produces small white flowers followed by white, red-freckled berries with a spicy, blueberry-like flavor over a long summer-to-fall season, forming a durable, drought-tolerant edible groundcover once its roots are established. It has almost no frost tolerance, so treat it as a container plant that can be moved under cover anywhere winter lows dip much below freezing. A light shearing after each fruiting flush keeps the mat dense and encourages the next round of flowers.
sources: Australian Native Food and Botanicals industry references

planting.note: Sow fresh seed (which loses viability quickly) directly from a fallen cone into a deep pot, since the large seed and long taproot resist transplanting once established; move seedlings to their permanent frost-free site after the first year, protecting young trees through their first several winters.

directions: Sow fresh seed straight from a fallen cone into a deep container, since the large nut and long taproot make this towering Australian conifer resent transplanting once it is well rooted. Bunya pine takes many years to reach flowering and cone-bearing size but rewards patient growers with basketball-sized cones containing dozens of large, chestnut-flavored nuts that are traditionally roasted or boiled. Give it a wide, open site well away from structures, parking, and foot traffic, because mature cones can weigh more than twenty pounds and drop from a great height without warning. Young trees tolerate a light frost but need full protection for their first several winters in the coolest parts of their growable range.
sources: Australian National Botanic Gardens plant profile
Queensland Department of Agriculture and Fisheries bushfood notes

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in late summer or early fall (or early spring in the coldest zones) at a shallow 1/4-inch depth; timothy establishes slowly and performs poorly on droughty soils.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed shallowly into a firm seedbed in late summer through early fall, or early spring in the coldest zones, since timothy establishes slowly and does poorly on droughty ground. It is the classic cool, humid-region hay and pasture grass, prized for palatability and curing quality and often seeded alongside red clover or alfalfa for a balanced hay mix. As a shallow-rooted bunchgrass it also works as a temporary cover crop between vegetable rotations, suppressing weeds and adding fibrous organic matter without becoming invasive. Mow or graze before full head emergence for the best forage quality and to encourage a thick, persistent stand.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Phleum pratense
University of Wisconsin Extension Forage Grasses

planting.note: Drill into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late fall for spring emergence, or in early spring in colder zones, at a shallow 1/2 to 1 inch depth; this native rhizomatous grass spreads via underground stems once established and grows slowly its first year while roots develop.

directions: Drill seed shallowly into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late fall or early spring, since this native rhizomatous grass spreads by underground stems once it has established and grows slowly through its first season. It is one of the most drought- and cold-hardy native sod formers on the Great Plains, used for erosion control, native pasture restoration, and valued for its blue-green color that persists through summer heat. Unlike introduced wheatgrasses it behaves well within native prairie plantings and pairs naturally with prairie legumes such as purple prairie clover. Avoid grazing or mowing until the second season while the rhizome network becomes established.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Pascopyrum smithii
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database
